blocks.text: Suppose point charges q1, q2, q3, ..., qn are arbitrarily distributed within an arbitrarily shaped closed surface (Fig. 9.14). Since the flux due to each charge is phi_e = q/eps0, the electric flux through the closed surface is phi_e = q1/eps0 + q2/eps0 + q3/eps0 + ... + qn/eps0 = (1/eps0) x (q1 + q2 + q3 + ... + qn) = (1/eps0) x (total charge enclosed by the closed surface), that is phi_e = (1/eps0) x Q ... (9.14), where Q = q1 + q2 + q3 + ... + qn is the total charge enclosed by the closed surface.

blocks.alt: An irregular pink closed surface containing seven small orange point charges labelled q1, q2, q3, q4, q5, q6 and qn.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.14 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.14).

blocks.title: Gauss's law
blocks.text: The total electric flux through any closed surface is 1/eps0 times the total charge enclosed in it.

Gauss's law can be applied to calculate the electric intensity due to different charge configurations. In all such cases an imaginary closed surface is considered which passes through the point at which the electric intensity is to be evaluated. This closed surface is known as a Gaussian surface; it is chosen so that the flux through it can be easily evaluated.
The field of a charged conducting sphere

Consider a conducting sphere of radius R carrying a charge q. All the charge is distributed uniformly over the surface of the sphere (Fig. 9.15). From the spherical symmetry the electric field is radial everywhere, and its magnitude depends only on the distance r from the centre; thus E is uniform over a spherical surface of any radius r concentric with the conductor. We take as our Gaussian surface an imaginary sphere of radius r greater than R.

blocks.alt: An inner circle (the conducting sphere, radius R, marked in cyan) with + charges on its surface, and a larger concentric circle (the Gaussian sphere, radius r). Magenta field lines run radially outward beyond both circles, dashed inside the conductor.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.15 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.15).

blocks.text: The area of the Gaussian sphere is 4 pi r^2, and because E is uniform over it, the total flux is phi_e = EA = E x 4 pi r^2. By Gauss's law, phi_e = q/eps0. Therefore E x 4 pi r^2 = q/eps0, or E = (q/eps0)(1/(4 pi r^2)) = (1/(4 pi eps0)) (q/r^2). This shows that the field at any point outside the sphere is the same as though the entire charge were concentrated at its centre. Just outside the sphere, where r = R, E = (1/(4 pi eps0)) q/R^2 ... (9.15); in vector form E = (1/(4 pi eps0)) (q/R^2) r (hat), where r (hat) is the direction of E.
